div.head: Preface
div.p: Didakta Grammar for Annotation

Didakta Grammar for Annotation is a localizable grammar reference for the ancient Greek language. Didakta has been developed by Farnoosh Shamsian at Leipzig University mainy through rearrangement and reformulation of H. W. Smyth's "Greek Grammar for Colleges" (1920), inspired by "Overview of Greek Syntax" by Jeffrey A. Rydberg-Cox (2000); however, some sections were revised based on recent publications such as the Cambridge Grammar of Classical Greek (Emde Boas et al., 2019).

Didakta Grammar for Annotation is primarily developed as a pedagogical resource to annotate syntactic difficulties that are not referenced in treebanks. While treebanks provide morphological and general syntactic data, Didakta provides more specific information to learners, for example, if a dative noun describes an instrument (e.g., “the hero was struck with a spear”) vs. a location (e.g., “the hero was struck on the shoulder”).

Didakta grammar is relatively modular, meaning that each section barely has a reference to the rest of the grammar and can be used independently. Additionally, the sequence of each section is not significant and can change according to the needs of each learner, course or project. Most importantly, it does not use positive language transfer to explain grammatical concepts. In other words, it does not leverage similarities between Ancient Greek and other languages known to the learners for teaching. Moreover, the text itself has been revised to avoid complex language to minimize inaccuracies in machine translation. Whenever possible, references to the Cambridge Grammar of Classical Greek (Emde Boas et al., 2019) and Pedalion Grammar (Van Hal et al., 2024) have been included in the footnotes.
Didakta is available in English, Persian, and Kurdish, and will soon be available in Portuguese. Further updates and relevant publications will be added to the Zenodo release description page.

div.head: §NomSubj SubjectSmyth 938-939, Pedalion 436, CGCG 30.02
div.p: The nominative case denotes the subject of the verb.

cit.quote: The delegates report these things to the soldiers
Proxenus was present

div.head: §NomPred PredicateSmyth 939, Pedalion 32, CGCG 30.03
div.p: The predicate noun in agreement of the subject of verbs such as εἰμί and γίγνομαι is in the nominative.

cit.quote: Clearchus was an exile
πᾶν ἐστὶ ἄνθρωπος συμφορή.
Man is entirely (a victim of) chance.

div.head: §NomInd IndependentSmyth 940-942, 904, CGCG 30.04, Pedalion 1078
div.p: The nominative may be used independently in citing the names of persons and things.

cit.quote: he received the common appellation of the vile, i.e. ‘informer’
τὸ δ᾽ ὑμεῖς ὅταν λέγω, λέγω τὴν πόλιν
when I say You, I mean the State

div.p: Independent nominatives are also used in incomplete sentences:

cit.quote: τίθημι δύο ποιητικῆς εἴδη: θεία μὲν καὶ ἀνθρωπίνη
I assume two kinds of poetry: the divine and the human

div.head: §NomVoc As VocativePedalion 33, CGCG 30.55
div.p: In a few cases, the nominative is used instead of a vocative for addressing or invoking.

cit.quote: O city, city!
Follow, slave, and bring my baggage.

div.head: §GenPos PossessorSmyth 1297-1302, Pedalion 292 and 115 , CGCG 30.28
div.p: The genitive denotes ownership, possession, or belonging. The genitive of possessor marks a person or thing that possesses someone or something else (and not the possessed). When referring to people, the genitive can denote the relationship of child to parent, wife to husband, or inferior to superior.

cit.quote: the expedition of Cyrus
the house of Simon
Thucydides, the son of Olorus
Artemis, daughter of Zeus
Melistiche wife of Smicythion
Lydus, the slave of Pherecles

div.p: The possessive genitive is used with the neuter article (singular or plural) denoting affairs, conditions, power, and the like:

cit.quote: (the function) of the art
(the maxim) of Solon
(the chances) of war are uncertain
(the interests) of the State

div.head: §GenPart PartitiveSmyth 1306-1319, Pedalion 118, CGCG 30.29
div.p: The genitive may express the general class to which a specific noun belongs. The partitive genitive or the genitive of the divided whole may be used with any word that expresses or implies a part.

cit.quote: the needy among the citizens
targeteers of the Thracians
few of them
whoever of the rest of the Greeks so desires
οἱ μὲν αὐτῶν, οἱ δ᾽ οὔ
some of them and not others
those of the enemy who were taken later
no one in the world
a part of the wall
one of the many things

div.head: §GenQual QualitySmyth 1320-1321, Pedalion 1041 & 124, CGCG 30.28
div.p: The genitive of quality denotes the quality of a person or thing and often is used as a predicate.

cit.quote: being of a peaceful disposition
but some few of the same opinion fled
this calls for a thorough discussion
θεωρήσατ᾽ αὐτόν, μὴ ὁποτέρου τοῦ λόγου, ἀλλ᾽ ὁποτέρου τοῦ βίου ἐστίν
consider, not the manner of his speech, but the manner of his life
if these matters seem to involve great expense and much toil and trouble

div.p: The attributive use occurs in poetry:

cit.quote: Europe with its pastures amid fair trees
a wing white as snow (of white snow)

div.head: §GenExpl ExplanationSmyth 1322, Pedalion 120, CGCG 30.28
div.p: The genitive of explanation, also called appositive genitive, adds specification or explanation to the meaning of a more general word. This construction is mostly used in poetry, but it can also be found in prose.

cit.quote: blasts of wind of every sort

quote.note: For more on this use of χρῆμα: Smyth 1294

cit.quote: a monster of a boar
the hill Istone

div.head: §GenMat MaterialSmyth 1323-1324, Pedalion 122, CGCG 30.28
div.p: The genitive of material expresses the composition or contents of a noun or specifies the material out of which something is made.

cit.quote: the fence (consisting) of the teeth
a spring of sweet water
σωροὶ σίτου, ξύλων, λίθων
heaps of corn, wood, stones
στεφάνους ῥόδων ὄντας, ἀλλ᾽ ου᾽ χρυσίου
crowns that were of roses, not of gold
a road was paved with stone

div.head: §GenMeas MeasureSmyth 1325-1327, Pedalion 971 & 780, CGCG 30.28
div.p: The genitive of measure denotes the extent in space, time or degree of a noun or its amount.

cit.quote: a wall eight stades long
provisions for five days
when a man is thirty years old
the walls were eight stades long
an income of two minae

div.head: §GenSubj SubjectiveSmyth 1330, Pedalion 125, CGCG 30.28
div.p: With nouns derived from verbs, the genitive may denote the subject of the action expressed in the noun. The subjective genitive is active in sense.

cit.quote: the fear of the barbarians (which they feel: οἱ βάρβαροι φοβοῦνται)
the perjury of the king (βασιλεὺς ἐπιορκεῖ)
Sing, o goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus

div.head: §GenObj ObjectiveSmyth 1331-1335, Pedalion 130, CGCG 30.28
div.p: The objective genitive denotes the object in a passive sense with nouns derived from verbs, and it is very common with nouns indicating a state of mind or an emotion:

cit.quote: the fear of the Helots (felt towards them: φοβοῦνται τοὺς Εἵλωτας）
good-will towards the Greeks (εὐνοεῖ τοῖς Ἕλλησι)
intercourse with the good (σύνεισι τοῖς καλοῖς)
war with the gods
oaths by the gods
anger at injustice
moderation in pleasure
speech with thee

div.head: §GenVal ValueSmyth 1336-1337, Pedalion 318 & 144, CGCG 30.31
div.p: The genitive of value denotes the value of a noun, such as price of an object. With verbs of buying, selling, costing or exchanging, the price given is in the genitive.

cit.quote: offerings worth three talents
I am defendant in an action involving a thousand drachmas
to buy or sell a horse for money
they deemed Themistocles worthy of the greatest gifts
I must not barter my public spirit for any price

div.head: §GenVerb Complement of the VerbSmyth 1341-1379, Smyth 1392-1407, Pedalion 977 & 302 & 121 & 166, , CGCG 30.21
div.p: Some verbs use the genitive as the object, such as verbs of sharing, beginning, aiming, attaining, remembering, smelling, touching, hearing, perceiving, filing, ruling, separating, releasing, depriving, commanding, etc. Many of these verbs can also take an accusative or dative object, with slight differences in meaning. Object of certain compound verbs (particularly those beginning with ἀπο-, ἐκ-, κατα-, προ- etc.) is in genitive. Furthermore, the objects in genitive could often be regarded as the genitive of source, cause, comparison, etc.

cit.quote: he was master of the sea
to cease from toil
knowledge divorced from justice
to be excluded from the forum
to save from evil
he deprives me of my property
all took part in the festival
to take a share of food
(ἡ νόσος) ἥψατο τῶν ἀνθρώπων
the plague laid hold of the men
he began his speech as follows
to aim at men
few tasted food
remember your absent friends
listening to the singer
I smell onions
to have plenty of provisions
he was master of the sea
he led the expedition

div.head: §GenSep Source and SeparationSmyth 1410-1411 & 1392 & 1298, Pedalion 783 & 303, CGCG 30.28 & 30.34
div.p: The genitive may indicate the place or point from which something is separated, particularly with words denoting motion or separation. Here may be classed the genitive of origin, indicating origin, source or offspring.

cit.quote: to cease from toil
knowledge divorced from justice”
wine was broached from the casks
obtaining this of you
learn this also from me
waves caused by all kinds of winds
of Darius and Parysatis are born two sons

div.head: §GenTime TimeSmyth 1444-1447, Pedalion 162, CGCG 30.32
div.p: The genitive denotes the time within which, or at a certain point of which, an action takes place. As contrasted with the accusative of time, the genitive signals a time frame for an action.

cit.quote: τὸν μὲν χειμῶνα ὕει ὁ θεός, τοῦ δὲ θέρεος χρηίσκονται τῷ ὕδατι
during the (entire) winter the god rains, but in (a part of) summer they need the water

div.p: The genitive may denote the time since an action has happened or the time until an action will happen:

cit.quote: for many years nobody has put a new question to me
the king will not fight for ten days

div.head: §GenComp ComparisonSmyth 1315-1316, Pedalion 146, CGCG 30.24
div.p: The genitive of comparison complements comparatives and superlatives as a standard of comparison.

cit.quote: the elder of us
the oldest of the generals
we make use of imported grain more than all other people

div.p: It is also used with a superlative adverb:

cit.quote: my ship was the best sailer of the whole squadron

div.head: §GenLoc PlaceSmyth 1448, Pedalion 149, CGCG 30.33
div.p: The genitive denotes the place within which or at which an action happens. This is more frequent in poetry than in prose.

cit.quote: to chase over the plain
having bathed in Oceanus
neither in sacred Pylos nor in Argos nor in Mycenae
thou didst admit this man within the walls
they dwell on the left hand (possibly ablatival).

div.head: §GenAbs In Genitive AbsoluteSmyth 2070-75, Pedalion 1099, CGCG 52.32
div.p: A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence stands in the genitive absolute. The noun or pronoun accompanying the participle expresses the subject:

cit.quote: these things were affected while Conon was in command
Ἠϊόνα . . . Μήδων ἐχόντων πολιορκίᾳ εἷλον
they blockaded and captured Eïon which was held by the Medes
the attendants led Cyrus inside at Astyages' bidding

div.head: §GenRef ReferenceSmyth 1380-81, Pedalion 300 & 320, CGCG 30.21
div.p: The genitive of reference is used with verbs of saying or thinking to state the subject and expresses a more or less close connection or relation to a subject.

cit.quote: τί δὲ ἵππων οἴει;
but what do you think of horses?
but tell me about my father
τοῦ κασιγνήτου τί φῄς;
what dost thou say of thy brother?
ἵππος ἢν κακουργῇ, τὸν ἱππέα κακίζομεν: τῆς δὲ γυναικός, εἰ κακοποιεῖ κτλ.
if a horse is vicious, we lay the fault to the groom; but as regards a wife, if she conducts herself ill, etc.
and so in the case of the other arts too
τί δὲ τῶν πολλῶν καλῶν;
what about the many beautiful things?

div.head: §GenCaus CauseSmyth 1375, 1405-9, Pedalion 141, CGCG 30.30
div.p: With verbs of emotion and dispute, the genitive denotes the cause. Such verbs are to wonder at, admire, envy, praise, blame, hate, pity, grieve for, be angry at, take vengeance on, and the like. The genitive of cause is closely connected with the genitive with verbs of disputing and verbs of judicial action.

cit.quote: I wondered at the hardihood of the speakers
admiring him for his mildness
ζηλῶ σε τοῦ νοῦ, τῆς δὲ δειλίας στυγῶ
I envy thee for thy prudence, I hate thee for thy cowardice
I thought you happy because of your disposition
it is right to praise the stranger for his zeal
he pitied him for his misery
he disputed the possession of the city with Erechtheus
to accuse one another of what had happened
Meletus prosecuted me for impiety
they were tried for bribery

div.head: §DatVerb Complement of the verbSmyth 1460-1470, Smyth 1544-1550, Pedalion 197 &182, CGCG 30.37
div.p: Dative expresses the indirect object of a verb, while the direct object is usually in accusative. The dative may be used as the object of many verbs, such as to benefit, help, injure, please, displease, be friendly or hostile, blame, be angry, threaten, envy, trust, believe, meet, obey, etc.

Object of certain compound verbs (in particular with σύν, ἐν, ἐπί, and with some compounded with παρά, περί, πρός, and ὑπό, etc.) is in dative, because the preposition keeps a sense that requires the dative. The objects in dative often could also be regarded as the dative of advantage, accompaniment, etc.

cit.quote: looking at him
to create expectations in men
the Greek force fell upon them
to be their accomplice in wrong-doing
obey the laws
the cities trusted him
he ordered the Mysian to flee
these did not join the king
to be subject to the ruler
he presented a horse to the Hyrcanian
to compare a small thing to a great thing
sending a messenger to him
he advised the Athenians as follows
he would not now be troubling us
they are angry at me
not cherishing envy against the rich
but when the generals met them
he meets Philocrates

div.head: §DatPos PossessorSmyth 1476-1480, CGCG 30.41, Pedalion 202
div.p: Dative denotes possession, belonging, or interest with verbs such as γίγνομαι and εἰμί. The person for whom a thing exists is put in the dative.

cit.quote: ἄλλοις μὲν χρήματά ἐστι, ἡμῖν δὲ ξύμμαχοι ἀγαθοί
others have riches, we have good allies
gifts are bestowed upon the just man by the gods
we have no supply of provisions

div.head: §DatAdvn Advantage (or Disadvantage)Smyth 1481-1486, Pedalion 185 & 188, CGCG 30.49
div.p: The person or thing for (or against) whom an action is done, is put in dative. With verbs which have no sense of advantage or disadvantage, the dative of advantage (or disadvantage) refers to the beneficiary or malefactive.

cit.quote: to be crowned in honour of the god
ἄλλῳ ὁ τοιοῦτος πλουτεῖ, καὶ οὐχ ἑαυτῷ
such a man is rich for another, and not for himself
after the barbarians had departed (for them, to their advantage) from their country
another army was being raised for him
Philistides was working in the interest of Philip
money is a cause of misery to mankind
ward off ruin from (for) the Danai

div.head: §DatEthic Ethical Dative (or Dative of Feeling)Smyth 1486-1487, CGCG, 30.53, Pedalion 192
div.p: A dative personal pronoun of the first and second person (μοι, ἡμῖν, σοι [or τοί], ὑμῖν) signals the interest of the speaker or the one being spoken to in the action of a statement and may also denote surprise. This dative is very rare in the third person. In many cases, ethical Dative (or Dative of Feeling) is left untranslated.

cit.quote: such a thing, you know, is despotism
pray remember not to make a disturbance
your young men will grow less cultivated
ὦ μῆτερ, ὡς καλός μοι ὁ πάππος
oh mother, how handsome grandpa is!

div.head: §DatAgent AgentSmyth 1488-1494, Pedalion 223, CGCG 30.50
div.p: With either verbal adjectives ending in -τός and -τέος or passive verbs in the perfect or pluperfect tenses, the dative of agent indicates the person in whose interest an action is done.

The notion of agency does not belong to the dative, but it is a natural inference that the person interested is the agent. The usual restriction of the dative to tenses of completed action seems to be due to the fact that the agent is represented as placed in the position of viewing an already completed action in the light of its relation to himself (interest, advantage, possession).

cit.quote: let so much have been said by me
has been done by (for) me and these men
when they had got their preparations ready
envied by those at home
we at least must struggle to defend our freedom

div.head: §DatMean Manner and meansSmyth 1527, Smyth 1507, Smyth 1372, Pedalion 229, CGCG 30.44
div.p: The dative, usually of an abstract noun, may indicate accompanying circumstance and manner or the means of an action. The datives of manner, means and attendant circumstances are sometimes similar to adverbs, for instance: βίᾳ by force, δίκῃ justly, δόλῳ by craft, (τῷ) ἔργῳ in fact, ἡσυχῇ quietly, σπουδῇ hastily, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ in truth, τῷ ὄντι in reality, ὀργῇ in anger.

cit.quote: they attacked with loud shouts
with all one's might
They ate in silence.
Hastily and with much noise they sailed their ships to Salamis.
βιαίῳ θανάτῳ ἀποθνῄσκειν” (= βίᾳ)
to die (by) a violent death.
to run at full speed

div.p: The dative of price and the dative of material and constituent parts may fall under this category:

cit.quote: they freed themselves from the danger at the price of a part of their unjust gains
he made chariots with strong wheels
they punished him by a fine

div.head: §DatMeas Measure of DifferenceSmyth 1513-1515, Pedalion 367, CGCG 30.54
div.p: With comparative adjectives, the dative marks the degree by which one thing differs from another. The dative of measure of difference indicates the extent of the difference and is used with comparatives or superlatives and other expressions of comparison.

cit.quote: a head shorter (lit. by the head)
he arrived not many days later
coming ten days before the Panathenaic festival
the shouting became much louder as the men increased in number
by far the best

div.head: §DatInstr InstrumentSmyth 1503-1511, Pedalion 216, CGCG 30.43
div.p: The dative of instrument expresses the instrument or tool by which or with which an action is done or accompanied. This use of the dative is the representative of the lost instrumental case.

cit.quote: he hit me with stone
he hurls his ax at him (hurls with his ax)
hacking them with their swords
defending themselves by pickets

div.head: §DatCaus Cause or PurposeSmyth 1473, 1517-19, CGCG 30.45
div.p: For the dative of purpose (to what end?), a predicate noun is used:
“ἐκείνῳ ἡ χώρα δῶρον ἐδόθη” X. H. 3.1.6; ⇾ the country was given to him as a gift
The dative, especially with verbs of emotion, expresses the occasion (external cause) or the motive (internal cause). Sometimes the dative of cause may resemble the dative of purpose.

cit.quote: the Athenians have set out against us (with a view to) to restore the Leontines
confident by reason of his good fortune
he was pleased at this
we were troubled at what had occurred
following out of friendship and good will
doing this out of insolence and not because he was drunk

div.head: §DatAccom Accompaniment Smyth 1524-1525, Pedalion 369, CGCG 30.51
div.p: The dative of accompaniment is used with verbs signifying to accompany or follow, mainly in military terminology. This meaning of dative is often equivalent to a dative of means outside the context of military terms.

cit.quote: to follow the leader
I am willing to follow you
he marches out with all his army

div.p: An extension of this usage occurs when the persons in the dative are essentially the same as the persons forming the subject (distributive use).

cit.quote: the enemy pursued us with their cavalry and peltasts

div.head: §DatTime TimeSmyth 1539-1543, CGCG 30.46, Pedalion 178 & 180
div.p: The dative without a preposition is commonly used to express an specific moment or period of time (chiefly day, night, month, year, season) at which an action occurred. The dative contrasts one point of time with another, and is usually accompanied by an attributive.

cit.quote: ταύτην μὲν τὴν ἡμέραν αὐτοῦ ἔμειναν, τῇ δὲ ὑστεραίᾳ κτλ.
throughout that day they waited there, but on the day following, etc.
in the third month
when summer was coming to an end
in the sixtieth year
in the winter season
at the Panathenaea
at the representations of the tragedies

div.head: §DatLoc PlaceSmyth 1530-1538, CGCG 30.47, Pedalion 170 & 173
div.p: In poetry the dative without a preposition is used to express the place where a person or thing is or where an action is taking place. In prose, the dative of place is limited to a few place names. This use of the dative is representative of the lost locative case.

cit.quote: taking his stand in the middle of the court
she lay on the ground
conspicuous among the Trojans
may be rose up among them (or for them).
fell on the ground
put thy sword into its sheath

div.head: §DatResp RespectSmyth 1516, Pedalion 240
div.p: The dative of respect indicates a thing in respect to which the verb or adjective is limited and is often nearly equivalent to the accusative of respect. The dative expresses the particular point of view from which a statement is made.

cit.quote: weak in body
a man still young in years
harsh of voice
distinguished in understanding
superior in power to the men of that time
a truce so far as the name goes

div.head: §DatExpr ExperiencerSmyth 1496-7, CGCG 30.52, Pedalion 203 & 204
div.p: The dative of a noun or pronoun can express the person in whose opinion a statement holds true or a situation or a direction is defined. The dative of experiencer is also common with impersonal verbs expressing emotions, necessity or need.

cit.quote: Darius contracted marriages most distinguished in the eyes of the Persians.
to be victorious in the judgment of all the judges
pitiful in the eyes of many
The council or the people or both decided

div.p: The dative participle, without a noun or pronoun, is frequently used in the singular or plural to denote indefinitely the person judging or observing. This construction is most common with participles of verbs of coming or going and with participles of verbs of considering.

cit.quote: Thrace is on the right as you sail into the Pontus
they said that, when you had crossed the river, the road led to Lydia
οὐκ οὖν ἄτοπον διαλογιζομένοις τὰς δωρεὰς νυνὶ πλείους εἶναι;
is it not strange, when we reflect, that gifts are more frequent now?
if you touched the surface the body was not very hot
if you look at the matter from the point of view of advantage, the panegyrist of justice speaks the truth

div.head: §AccObj Direct ObjectSmyth 1553-1555, CGCG 30.8, Pedalion 51
div.p: Accusative is used as the direct object with verbs which take an object.

cit.quote: I see the man
Everyone praises the man
I am ashamed of my lowly descent.

div.head: §AccCog CognateSmyth 1563-1577, CGCG 30.12, Pedalion 342
div.p: The cognate accusatives are objects added to specify the nature of the action of the verb and are either etymologically or semantically related to the verb. They can be nouns in the accusative that are of the same origin as the verb (they contain the same stem), or of kindred meaning with the verb (they express the same meaning). In many cases, the cognate accusative is left untranslated to avoid redundancy.

cit.quote: talking much nonsense
he shared in the recent exile
victorious in the sea-fight at Salamis
the promises which he made
the charge they bring
war was waged
war was stirred up

div.head: §AccSubj Subject of Infinitive or ParticipleSmyth 1972-1981, CGCG 30.11, Pedalion 1006
div.p: The accusative can express the subject in an infinitive or participle clause. When the subject of the infinitive is different from that of the governing verb, it stands in the accusative; and a predicate noun stands also in the accusative. When the subject of the infinitive is the same as the subject or object of the governing verb, or when it has already been made known in the sentence, it is rarely repeated with the infinitive.

cit.quote: for I think you are to me both fatherland and friends
for I maintain that the noble and good man is happy
I think I have made more money than any two others together
he issued orders that the Greeks should get under arms

div.head: §AccResp RespectSmyth 1600-1605, CGCG 30.14, Pedalion 92 & 820
div.p: The accusative of respect or limitation expresses a thing in respect to which the verb or adjective is limited. The accusative usually expresses a local relation or the instrument. The word restricted by the accusative of respect usually indicates like or similar to, good or better, bad or worse, a physical or a mental quality, or an emotion. The accusative of respect often specifies qualities and attributes (nature, form, size, name, birth, number, etc.), or it may indicate the sphere in general and is added to verbs denoting a state, and to adjectives.

cit.quote: you are blind in ears, and mind, and eyes
the man has a pain in his finger
swift-footed Achilles
woman differs from man in nature
about two thousand in number
tell me of what race thou art
terrible in battle
transfer yourselves in thought

div.head: §AccTime TimeSmyth 1582-1587, CGCG 30.15, Pedalion 87
div.p: The accusative of time indicates duration and the extent of time. It implies that the action of the verb covers the entire period.

cit.quote: he remained seven days
they made an alliance for a hundred years

div.p: To mark how long a situation has lasted or how much time has elapsed since something happened, an ordinal is used without the article, but often with the addition of οὑτοσί. The current day or year is included. Thus:

cit.quote: my mother who died two years ago
he has been in the city since day before yesterday
this is the third or fourth year since it was announced that Philip was besieging fort Heraeum

div.head: §AccSpac SpaceSmyth 1581, CGCG 30.16, Pedalion 84
div.p: The accusative of space expresses a space, distance or path. It denotes the space or way over which an action is extended, or the measure of the space traversed.

cit.quote: ἄγειν (στρατιὰν) στενὰς ὁδούς
to lead an army over narrow roads
ἐξελαύνει σταθμοὺς τρεῖς, παρασάγγας εἴκοσι καὶ δύο
he advances three stages, twenty- two parasangs
Plataea is seventy stades distant from Thebes

div.head: §AccDirec DirectionSmyth 1588, CGCG 30.17, Pedalion 75
div.p: In poetry, the accusative may be used without a preposition to express the goal after verbs of motion.

cit.quote: having come to the city of Cadmus
we will convey her to Greece

div.p: Of persons in Homer (especially with ἱκνέομαι, ἵκω, ἱκάνω \= reach) and in the lyric parts of the drama:

cit.quote: came unto the suitors

div.head: §AccAdv AdverbialSmyth 1606-1611, Pedalion 95 & 105, CGCG 30.18
div.p: Many accusatives marking limitations of the verbal action serve the same function as adverbs.

Expressing manner: τρόπον τινά in some way, τίνα τρόπον in what way? τόνδε (τοῦτον) τὸν τρόπον in this way, πάντα τρόπον in every way (also παντὶ τρόπῳ), τὴν ταχίστην (ὁδόν) in the quickest way, τὴν εὐθεῖαν (ὁδόν) straightforward.

cit.quote: like an archer
he sailed professedly for the Hellespont

div.p: Many adverbial accusatives express measure and degree: μέγα, μεγάλα greatly, πολύ, πολλά much, τὸ πολύ, τὰ πολλά for the most part, ὅσον as much as, οὐδέν, μηδέν not at all, τοσοῦτον so much, τὶ somewhat, ἀρχήν or τὴν ἀρχήν at all with οὐ or μή.

cit.quote: it is utterly impossible to deliberate correctly offhand

div.head: §AccOath OathsSmyth 1596, Pedalion 818
div.p: The accusative of oath indicates the person or thing by which one swears and is accompanied bythe adverbs of swearing such as μά, οὐ μά, ναὶ μά, νή, or verbs of swearing, ὀμνύναι swear by (τοὺς θεούς, pass. Ζεὺς ὀμώμοται) and swear to (τὸν ὅρκον, pass. ὁ ὅρκος ὀμώμοται).

cit.quote: I swear to you by all the gods and goddesses.

div.p: μά is negative, except when preceded by ναί. μά may stand alone when a negative precedes (often in a question) or when a negative follows in the next clause:

cit.quote: μὰ τὸν Ἀπόλλω, οὔκ
No, by Apollo

div.p: μά is sometimes omitted after οὐ, and after ναί:

cit.quote: by heaven, [you wil] not.

div.head: §AccDoubl Double AccusativeSmyth 1619-1635, CGCG 30.9, Pedalion 357 & 360 & 108
div.p: In addition to a direct object, several verbs take a compliment in the accusative. Double accusatives are common with the verbs meaning to do, to demand, to ask, to name or call, to choose, to persuade, etc. The second accusative could also be internal object (see AccCog.).

cit.quote: He recounted how many good things Cyrus had done to the Persians.
he appointed him general
you were wont to call me father
they elected Timotheus general
he has made himself master
if you make me your servant
showing yourself a sophist before the Greeks
that's not the question I'm asking you
he concealed from his daughter her husband's death
to ask Cyrus for boats
I cannot persuade you of this
I will remind you of the dangers also

div.head: §AccCaus Cause or GoalSmyth 1610, Pedalion 96 & 100
div.p: The accusative could express the cause as a neuter pronoun indicating a situation. Many of these pronouns are very idiomatic: τί; 'why?, wherefore?' τοῦτο, ταῦτα 'for this reason'. The difference with the accusative of goal is very small.

cit.quote: For these reasons I have left the gold-decorated palace.
τί δέ; … - ἵνα ἤκουσας ἀνδρῶν διαλεγομένων οἳ νῦν σοφώτατοί εἰσι
Why was that? So that you could hear men who are the wisest at the moment.
for this very reason have I come
for this reason you are vexed

div.p: With χάριν for the sake of (lit. favour):

cit.quote: did not engage in the expedition out of good will to the Athenians
for what reason?
for thy sake I have come

div.head: §Voc Exclamations and direct addressSmyth 1283-1288, CGCG 30.55, Pedalion 38 & 49
div.p: The vocative is used in exclamations and in direct address:

cit.quote: oh Zeus and ye gods
my good fellow

div.p: In ordinary conversation and public speeches, the polite ὦ is usually added. Without ὦ the vocative may express astonishment, joy, contempt, a threat, or a warning, etc.:

cit.quote: ἀκούεις Αἰσχίνη;
d'ye hear, Aeschines?

div.p: But this distinction is not always observed, though in general ὦ has a familiar tone which was unsuited to elevated poetry.

div.head: §Pres Present of ContinuitySmyth 1875 & 1879-1882, CGCG 33.14
div.p: The present represents a present state, or an action going on at the moment of speaking. The action might have begun before the present time. The present tense has an imperfective aspect and therefore often indicates incomplete actions. It may also indicate immediate future, or likely and certain actions in the near future. In prophecies a future event may be regarded as present.

cit.quote: I am telling the truth
μεταξὺ τὸν λόγον καταλύομεν;
shall we break off in the middle?
καὶ εἰ βούλει, παραχωρῶ σοι τοῦ βήματος, ἕως ἂν εἴπῃς
and if you wish, I will yield you the floor until you tell us
I am on the verge of ruin
εἰ αὕτη ἡ πόλις ληφθήσεται, ἔχεται καὶ ἡ πᾶσα Σικελία
if this city is taken, the whole of Sicily as well is in their power
in time this expedition will capture Priam's city

div.head: §PresIter Customary Action (Iterative)Smyth 1876-1877, CGCG 33.15
div.p: The present is used to express a customary or repeated action:

cit.quote: οὗτος μὲν γὰρ ὕδωρ, ἐγὼ δ᾽ οἶνον πίνω
for this man drinks water, whereas I drink wine

div.p: The present indicative may also indicate a general truth and could be used to express an action that is true for all time. The present is an absolute tense in such sentences. The future, aorist, and perfect may also express a general truth.

cit.quote: two times five is ten
time brings the truth to light

div.head: §PresCona Conative PresentSmyth 1878, CGCG 33.17 & 33.54
div.p: The present may express an action begun, attempted, or intended. The idea of attempt or intention is an inference from the context and lies in the present only so far as the present does not denote completion.

cit.quote: they are trying to persuade you to throw away this renown
I offer you this woman herself as a wife
they are trying to betray Greece

div.head: §PresHist Historical PresentSmyth 1883-1884, CGCG 33.20
div.p: In lively or dramatic narration, the present is used to represent a past action as going on at the moment of speaking or writing. The historical present may represent either the descriptive imperfect or the narrative aorist. This use does not occur in Homer.

cit.quote: ὁ δὲ Θεμιστοκλῆς φεύγει ἐς Κέρκυραν . . . διακομίζεται ἐς τὴν ἤπειρον
Themistocles fled (flees) to Corcyra . . . was (is) transported to the mainland

div.p: Closely connected with the historical present is the annalistic present, which is used to register historical facts or to note incidents.

cit.quote: of Darius and Parysatis were (are) born two sons
καὶ ὁ ἐνιαυτὸς ἔληγεν, ἐν ᾧ Καρχηδόνιοι αἱροῦσι δύο πόλεις Ἑλληνίδας
and the year came to an end in which the Carthaginians captured two Greek cities

div.head: §PresPerf Resultative and Perfective PresentSmyth 1886-1888, CGCG 33.18 & 33.20
div.p: The present of certain verbs often expresses an enduring result, and may be translated by the perfect: ἀδικῶ I am guilty (ἄδικός εἰμι), I have done wrong, νικῶ, κρατῶ, I am victorious, I have conquered, ἡττῶμαι I am conquered, φεύγω I am the defendant or I am an exile, προδίδωμι I am a traitor, ἁλίσκομαι I am captured, στέρομαι I am deprived, γίγνομαι I am a descendant.

The perfective present is common with verbs of hearing, saying, learning, whose action commenced in the past, but whose effect continues into the present. The present tense with telic verbs has a resultative meaning, such as ἥκω I am come, I have arrived, οἴχομαι I am gone, etc. The present may also indicate an action begun in the past and continued in the present. This use of present tense is accompanied by a definite or indefinite expression of past time.

cit.quote: I Themistocles have come to you
I know where they have gone
I have been long (and am still) wondering
from what I hear (have heard)
as I said

div.head: §PresNoni Non-indicative (Imperfective Aspect)Smyth 1859-67, 1872, CGCG 30.4-7
div.p: The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the grammatical aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates how an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The present stem has an imperfective aspect, generally expressing actions as ongoing or repeated.
With subjunctive:

cit.quote: let us at the same time keep developing our resources

div.p: With optative:

cit.quote: may I (always) count the wise man wealthy

div.p: With Imperative, implying continuance:

cit.quote: honour thy parents
tell (go on and tell in detail) the whole truth
offer the horses to them

div.p: With Participles: The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated. The action is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb.

cit.quote: ἐργαζόμεναι μὲν ἠρίστων, ἐργασάμεναι δὲ ἐδείπνουν
the women took their noonday meal while they continued their work, but took their supper when they had stopped work
the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence

div.p: With infinitives:

cit.quote: οὐδὲ βουλεύεσθαι ἔτι ὥρα, ἀλλὰ βεβουλεῦσθαι
it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up

div.head: §Impf Imperfect of ContinuanceSmyth 1890-1892 & 1896-97, CGCG 33.22
div.p: The imperfect represents an action as ongoing in the past.

cit.quote: διέφθειραν Ἀθηναίων πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι, οἳ ξυνεπολιορκοῦντο
they put to death twenty-five of the Athenians who were besieged (i.e. from the beginning to the end of the siege)
Antiochus was reigning

div.p: The imperfect of verbs of sending, going, saying, exhorting, etc., which imply continuous action, is often used where one might expect the aorist of concluded action. Thus, in ἔπεμπον, the action is regarded as unfinished since the goal is not reached.

cit.quote: they sent a messenger and surrendered the dead under a truce

div.p: With a negative, the imperfect often denotes resistance or refusal (would not or could not), while the negative aorist denotes unrestricted denial of a fact.

cit.quote: you would not accept the proposal (compare to: τὴν ἱκετείαν οὐκ ἐδέξαντο T.1. 24; ⇾ they did not receive the supplication)
ὁ μὲν οὐκ ἐγάμει, ὁ δὲ ἔγημεν
the one would not marry, the other did
οὐδὲ φωνὴν ἤκουον, εἴ τις ἄλλο τι βούλοιτο λέγειν
they would not even listen to a syllable if ever any one wished to say anything to the contrary

div.head: §ImpfIter Customary Action (Iterative)Smyth 1893-1895, CGCG 33.24
div.p: The imperfect is used to express frequently repeated or customary past actions. ἄν may be used with this imperfect to express the repetition emphatically. Homer and Herodotus have iterative imperfects and aorists stems in -σκον and -σκομην denoting a customary or repeated past action.

cit.quote: ἐπεὶ εἶδον αὐτὸν οἵπερ πρόσθεν προσεκύνουν, καὶ τότε προσεκύνησαν
when they caught sight of him, the very men who before this were wont to prostrate themselves before him, prostrated themselves on this occasion also
(Σωκράτης) τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιθυμοῦντας οὐκ ἐπράττετο χρήματα
Socrates was not in the habit of demanding money from those who were passionately attached to him
people would (used to) desire to hear still more from him
I used to ask

div.head: §ImpfCona Conative ImperfectSmyth 1895, CGCG 33.25
div.p: The imperfect may express an action attempted, intended, or expected in the past that eventually did not occur. The conative imperfect is used with telic verbs.

cit.quote: ἔπειθον αὐτούς, καὶ οὓς ἔπεισα, τούτους ἔχων ἐπορευόμην
I tried to persuade them, and I marched away with those whom I succeeded in persuading
Ἁλόννησον ἐδίδου: ὁ δ᾽ ἀπηγόρευε μὴ λαμβάνειν
Philip offered (proposed to give) Halonnesus, but he (Demosthenes) dissuaded them from accepting it
the Thebans tried to enslave them
they were for pushing on to Corcyra

div.head: §ImpfComp Imperfect of Completed ActionSmyth 1906, CGCG 33.51
div.p: The imperfect with telic verbsA telic verb describes an activity or event as having a specific endpoint, while an atelic verb does not necessarily have a particular endpoint. draws attention toward the consequences of the action, while the present of these verbs suggests that the action is not completed yet. Thus, ἧκον I had come (rarely I came), ᾠχόμην I had departed, as ἐνίκων I was victorious, ἡττώμην I was defeated.

cit.quote: ὃ μὲν δή σφι τὰ ἐντεταλμένα ἀπήγγελλε, τοῖσι δὲ ἕαδε μὲν βοηθέειν Ἀθηναίοισι ...
He delivered the message he had been ordered to say, and they resolved to send help to the Athenians
(Ὀλύμπια) οἷς Ἀνδροσθένης παγκράτιον ἐνίκα
the Olympic games, at which Androsthenes was the victor (= had won) in the pancratium
τὸ πλοῖον ἧκεν, ἐν ᾧ ἐπλέομεν
the vessel arrived in which we (had) sailed

div.head: §ImpfDesc Imperfect of DescriptionSmyth 1898-1907, GCGC 33.51
div.p: The imperfect can explain the background circumstances under which an action has taken place. It describes manners and customs; the situation, circumstances, and details of events; and the development of actions represented as continuing in past time. The imperfect often has a dramatic or panoramic force: it enables the reader to follow the course of events as they occurred, as if he were a spectator of the scene depicted.

cit.quote: εὐθὺς ἀνεβόησάν τε πάντες καὶ προσπεσόντες ἐμάχοντο, ἐώθουν, ἐωθοῦντο, ἔπαιον, ἐπαίοντο
immediately all raised a shout and falling upon each other fought, pushed and were pushed, struck and were struck
ἐπεὶ δὲ ταῦτα ἐρρήθη, ἐπορεύοντο: τῶν δὲ ἀπαντώντων οἱ μὲν ἀπέθνῃσκον, οἱ δὲ ἔφευγον πάλιν εἴσω, οἱ δὲ ἐβόων
and when these words had been spoken, they proceeded to advance; and of those who met them some were killed, others fled back indoors, and others shouted

div.p: In descriptions of places and scenery and in other statements of existing facts the imperfect is often used by assimilation to the time of the narrative (usually set forth in the main verb).

cit.quote: they came to the river which divided the country of the Macrones from that of the Scytheni
ἐξελαύνει ἐπὶ ποταμὸν πλήρη ἰχθύων, οὓς οἱ Σύροι θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον
he marched to a river full of fish, which the Syrians regarded as gods

div.p: The imperfect may refer to a topic previously discussed. This is called the philosophical imperfect:

cit.quote: music is (as we have seen) the counterpart of gymnastics, if you remember the discussion

div.head: §ImpfCons Imperfect of Consecutive ActionSmyth 1900, CGCG 33.52
div.p: The imperfect may refer to an action that immediately follows another action. This use of imperfect is sometimes referred to as inchoative or inceptive imperfect; however, this use of imperfect does not exactly refer the beginning point of an action , but it expressses the action in process.

cit.quote: ἐπειδὴ δὲ καιρὸς ἦν, προσέβαλλον
but when the proper time arrived, they began an (proceeded to) attack
ὡς δὲ πορευομένων ἐξεκύμαινέ τι τῆς φάλαγγος, τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον ἤρξατο δρόμῳ θεῖν: καὶ ἅμα ἐφθέγξαντο πάντες οἷον τῷ Ἐνυαλίῳ ἐλελίζουσι, καὶ πάντες δὲ ἔθεον

And when, as they proceeded, a part of the phalanx billowed out, those who were thus left behind began to run; at the same moment they all set up the sort of war-cry which they raise to Enyalius, and next, they were all running.

div.head: §Fut Future Events or ExpectationsSmyth 1910-1913, CGCG 33.43
div.p: The future denotes an action that will take place at some future time. The future tense indicates that according to the opinion, expectation, hope, fear, or purpose of the speaker or the agent, the action would happen in the future. Depending on the context, the action of the future could be both continuative (like the present) or, similar to the aorist, express simple attainment. For instance, πείσω means I shall try to persuade, or I shall convince (resultative), βασιλεύσω I shall be king, shall reign or I shall become king (ingressive).

cit.quote: he shall receive a talent as his reward
Θηβαῖοι ἔχουσι μὲν ἀπεχθῶς, ἔτι δ᾽ ἐχθροτέρως σχήσουσιν
the Thebans are hostile and will become still more so

div.head: §FutHypo Hypothesis or General TruthSmyth 1914-1916, CGCG 33.45
div.p: The future may be used to express an action possible in the moment of speaking, hypothetical scenarios, inferences, or present intention. In this sense, instead of indicating that the action would happen in the actual future, the future tense implies that the statement could be verified in the future.

cit.quote: εὑρήσομεν τοὺς φιλοτίμους τῶν ἀνδρῶν . . . ἀντὶ τοῦ ζῆν ἀποθνῄσκειν εὐκλεῶς αἱρουμένους
we shall find that ambitious men choose a glorious death in preference to life
αἶρε πλῆκτρον, εἰ μαχεῖ
raise your spur if you mean to fight
τί λέξεις;
what do you mean?

div.p: The future may indicate a general truth (also known as gnomic future).

cit.quote: a reasonable man, if he loses a son, will (is expected to) bear it more easily than other men

div.p: The future tense in commonly used in deliberative questions:

cit.quote: what shall we say or what shall we propose?

div.head: §FutJuss Jussive FutureSmyth 1917-1922, CGCG 38.32 & 33.44
div.p: The future in the second person may function similar to the imperative, and express an urgent command, prohibition, concession or permission. The tone of the jussive future is generally familiar. In combination with οὐ μή , it indicates urgent prohibition. This use of the future tense is post-homeric.

cit.quote: you will do thus
ἀναγνώσεται τὸν νόμον—ἀναγίγνωσκε
the clerk will read the law—read
you will judge for yourself
you will have to hurry on the march
ὑμεῖς οὖν, ἐὰν σωφρονῆτε, οὐ τούτου ἀλλ᾽ ὑμῶν φείσεσθε
now, if you are wise, you will spare, not him, but yourselves

div.head: §FutNoni Non-indicativeSmyth 1859-68, 1872, CGCG 33.4-7 & 52.4 & 52.41
div.p: The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the grammatical aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates the way an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The future stem does not have an aspectual value, meaning that it is neutral and makes no distinction between completed or imperfect actions. The future participle refers to an action posterior to the main verb.
With participles: The future participle is often voluntative and expresses purpose. In combination with ὡς, it indicates the intention of the subject.

cit.quote: we have not come together for the purpose of waging war with the king
they prepared themselves for wage war

div.p: The verb ἔρχομαι with future participle is idiomatic, and often translates to “about to” or “going to”.

cit.quote: ἐγὼ δὲ περὶ μὲν τούτων οὐκ ἔρχομαι ἐρέων ὡς …
About these matters, I am not going to say that ...

div.p: With infinitives: When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist.

cit.quote: not being able to prevent
I am far from intending to speak to my own disadvantage

div.head: §Aor Resultative AoristSmyth 1923-1929, CGCG 33.28
div.p: The aorist expresses the mere occurrence of an action in the past. The action is regarded as an event or single fact without reference to the length of time it occupied. As a narrative tense it is often used to state the chief events and facts, while the other past tenses set forth subordinate actions and attendant circumstances. In contrast to the imperfect (and present) the aorist denotes the result, end, or effect of an action.

cit.quote: the Corcyraeans were victorious and destroyed fifteen ships
and after he posted watchers he called the troops together and spoke as follows

div.p: The same verb may be a resultative aorist or an ingressive aorist; for instance, ἔβαλον I let fly a missile (ingressive), and I hit (resultative); κατέσχον I got possession of (ingressive), and I kept back (resultative).

div.head: §AorIngr Ingressive AoristSmyth 1924-1925, CGCG 33.29
div.p: The aorist of verbs whose present denotes a state or a continued action, expresses the entrance into that state or the beginning of that action. The ingressive aorist is used with atelic verbsA telic verb describes an activity or event as having a specific endpoint, while an atelic verb does not necessarily have a particular endpoint., particularly with stative verbs and indicates the beginning of a state; for instance, ἄρχω rule: ἦρξα became ruler, βασιλεύω am king, rule: ἐβασίλευσα became king, ascended the throne, or νοσῶ am ill: ἐνόσησα fell ill.

cit.quote: καί οἱ πάντα τε ἐκεῖνα διδοῖ καὶ πρὸς ἕτερα δωρέεται οὐκ ἐλάσσω ἐκείνων. οὕτω μὲν ἐπλούτησε ἡ οἰκίη αὕτη μεγάλως
and he gave him all those things and gifted him much more again, thus the family grew very rich
when Peisistratus died Hippias succeeded to his power

div.head: §AorComp Complexive AoristSmyth 1927-1929, CGCG 33.30
div.p: The complexive aorist is used to survey at a glance the course of a past action from beginning to end and often is accompanied with an expression of the duration. It may sum up the result of a preceding narrative. This is often called the concentrative aorist, because it concentrates the entire course of an action to a single point.

cit.quote: it was in this manner that they fortified the city
the peace lasted fourteen years
the league lasted a short time
Cyrus remained thirty days there

div.head: §AorGnom Gnomic AoristSmyth 1931-1932 & 1935, CGCG 33.31
div.p: Gnomic aorist (γνώμη maxim, proverb) indicates a general truth. This use of the aorist does not seem to simply states a past occurrence, but it expresses habits, general tendencies, procedures, or typical events.

cit.quote: a fool learns by experience
for beauty is either wasted by time or withered by disease

div.p: Akin to the gnomic aorist is the aorist employed in general descriptions, imaginary scenes and in descriptions of manners and custom. The aorist is used in similes in poetry, and usually contains the point of comparison.

cit.quote: ἐπειδὰν ἀφίκωνται οἱ τετελευτηκότες εἰς τὸν τόπον, οἷ ὁ δαίμων ἕκαστον κομίζ πρῶτον μὲν διεδικάσαντο οἵ τε καλῶς καὶ ὁσίως βιώσαντες καὶ οἱ μή
when the dead reach the place whither each is severally conducted by his genius, first of all the have judgment pronounced upon them as they have lived well and devoutly not
after having woven a mantle on the same day the pries bind the eyes of one of their number with a snood
he fell as falls an oak

div.head: §AorSug Suggestive Questions and RequestsSmyth 1934-1936, CGCG 33.33
div.p: The aorist is used in questions with τί οὖν ου and τί οὐ to express surprise that something has not been done. The question is here equivalent to a command or a suggestion.

cit.quote: τί οὖν οὐχὶ καὶ σὺ ὑπέμνησάς με;
why don't you recall it to my mind?
τί οὖν οὐ διηγήσω ἡμῖν τὴν συνουσίαν, εἰ μή σέ τι κωλύει…
let us hear your account of the conversation at once, if nothing prevents you

div.head: §AorIter Customary Action (Iterative)Smyth 1933 & 495, CGCG 33.24
div.p: The aorist with ἄν may indicate repetitions and habits. Additionally, Homer and Herodotus have iterative imperfects and aorists in -σκον and -σκομην denoting a customary or repeated past action. Homer has iterative forms in the imperfect and 1 and 2 aorist active and middle. Herodotus has no iteratives in the 1 aorist and few in the 2 aorist.

cit.quote: he used to say
he was wont to say
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι φύγεσκε βαθείης βένθεσιν ὕλης κνώδαλον, ὅττι δίοιτο
no creature that he started in the depths of the thick wood could escape him

div.head: §AorDram Dramatic AoristSmyth 1937, CGCG 33.32
div.p: The first person singular of the aorist is used in the answers and reactions in tragedy and comedy, often indicating a state of mind or an act expressing a state of mind (especially approval or disapproval) occurring to the speaker in the moment just passed. The dramatic aorist is sometimes called instantaneous aorist.

cit.quote: ἥσθην, ἐγέλασα
I am delighted, I can't help laughing
I welcome the omen

div.p: Sometimes this use appears outside of dialogue:

cit.quote: I spurn

div.head: §AorNoni Non-indicative (Perfective Aspect)Smyth 1859-67, 1872-3, CGCG 33.4-7
div.p: The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates the way an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The aorist has a perfective aspect, presenting the verb as completed, or an uninterrupted whole.
With Subjunctive:

cit.quote: let us procure the money first

div.p: With optative:

cit.quote: would that it might happen

div.p: With imperatives, indicating simple occurrence:

cit.quote: look (cast a glance) toward the mountains
give the horses to us

div.p: With Infinitives:

cit.quote: the desire of obtaining drink
began to be

div.p: With Participles:

cit.quote: after supper he advanced
after killing the free men they withdrew
he took an oath and said
Σάτυρος καὶ Χρέμων, οἱ τῶν τριάκοντα γενόμενοι, Κλεοφῶντος κατηγόρουν
Satyrus and Chremon, who (afterwards) became members of the Thirty, accused Cleophon

div.head: §Perf Completed actionSmyth 1945-1946, CGCG 33.34 & 33.36
div.p: The perfect denotes a completed action the effects of which still continue in the present:

cit.quote: the rooms have been constructed (their construction is finished)
he has taken away (and still holds) their cities
τί βουλεύεσθον ποιεῖν; οὐδέν, ἔφη ὁ Χαρμίδης, ἀλλὰ βεβουλεύμεθα
what are you conspiring to do? Nothing, said Charmides; we have already conspired

div.p: “ἐφοβήθην, καὶ ἔτι καὶ νῦν τεθορύβημαι” Aes. 2.4; ⇾ I was struck with fear, and even at the present moment am still in a state of agitation

When the perfect marks the enduring result rather than the completed act, it may not indicate any clear reference to the preceding action; for instance, κέκλημαι (have received a name) am called, my name is, κέκτημαι (have acquired) possess, μέμνημαι (have recalled) remember, τέθνηκα (have passed away) am dead, οἶδα (have found out) know. These are often translated to a present tense and therefore, they are sometimes called “perfect with present meaning”; however, they are not fundamentally different from other perfect verbs.

div.head: §PerfInten Intensive PerfectSmyth 1947, CGCG 33.37 & 33.35
div.p: The perfects tense with atelic verbsA telic verb describes an activity or event as having a specific endpoint, while an atelic verb does not necessarily have a particular endpoint. may indicate an emphasis of the degree of the state expressed by the verb. These are often called intensive perfects. Such are: verbs of the senses (δέδορκα gaze, πέφρικα shudder), of sustained sound (κέκραγα bawl, λέληκα shout, βέβρυχα roar), of emotion (πεφόβημαι am filled with alarm, γέγηθα am glad, μέμηλε cares for), of gesture (κέχηνα keep the mouth agape), and many others (σεσίγηκα am still, etc.).

cit.quote: πολλὰ δὲ θαυμάζων τῶν εἰωθότων λέγεσθαι παρ᾽ ὑμῖν, οὐδενὸς ἧττον, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, τεθαύμακα, ὃ καὶ πρώην τινὸς ἤκουσ᾽ εἰπόντος ἐν τῇ βουλῇ
I often wonder at the sort of speeches that are delivered here, but nothing, men of Athens, has surprised me more than what I heard uttered in the Council the other day

div.p: With certain telic verbs, the perfect tense may emphasize the responsibility of the subject for the results of the verb.

cit.quote: the same Thucydides of Athens is the author of this a well.

div.head: §PerfFut Perfect for Future PerfectSmyth 1950, CGCG 33.38
div.p: The perfect may be used instead of the future perfect to anticipate an action that has not occurred yet; however, it is presented as already having had an effect . This use of the perfect tense is sometimes called the rhetorical perfect.

cit.quote: κἂν τοῦτο νικῶμεν, πάνθ᾽ ἡμῖν πεποίηται
and if we conquer in that quarter, everything has been (will have been) accomplished by us

div.p: Especially with the phrase τὸ ἐπί τινι, the perfect anticipates the certain occurrence of an event:

cit.quote: for all he could do, we had perished

div.head: §PerfNoni Non-indicativeSmyth 1859-67, 1872, CGCG 33.4-7
div.p: The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates the way an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The perfect in non-indicative verbs presents the action as a state and emphasizes on the effect or results of an action that has already happened.
With subjunctive:

cit.quote: ἵνα, ἢν μὴ ὑπακούωσι, τεθνήκωσιν
that, in case they do not submit, they may be put to death (lit. may be dead at once)

div.p: With optative: In the optative, the reference is always to future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.

cit.quote: τεθναίης ὦ Προῖτ᾽, ἢ κάκτανε Βελλεροφόντην
either die thyself, Proetus, or slay Bellerophon

div.p: With Imperative, indicating completion with permanent result:

cit.quote: let him take his place (and stay there)
let it have been said (once for all)

div.p: With infinitives, often of certainty of action:

cit.quote: οὐδὲ βουλεύεσθαι ἔτι ὥρα, ἀλλὰ βεβουλεῦσθαι
it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up

div.p: With Participles:

cit.quote: they found (historical present) that Brasidas had arrived

div.p: A perfect participle may have the force of a pluperfect if accompanied by an adverb like πρόσθεν:

cit.quote: he who possessed it before

div.head: §Pperf Past PerfectSmyth 1952-1953, CGCG 33.11 & 33.40 & 33.50
div.p: The pluperfect is the past of the perfect, therefore, it indicates a past fixed state resulting from a completed action. Unlike many other languages, Greek does not necessarily need to use pluperfect for expressing an action that happened prior to an aforementioned time in the past, and it can use the aspectual value of other past tenses for this purpose. The pluperfect expresses absolute tense.

cit.quote: the Indians returned whom Cyrus had sent to get news of the enemy

div.p: Similar to imperfect, the pluperfect is also used for describing the background circumstances of an action:

cit.quote: φθάνουσι τῶν Πλαταιῶν καὶ οἱ ὕστατοι διαβάντες τὴν τάφρον, χαλεπῶς δὲ καὶ βιαίως: κρύσταλλός τε γὰρ ἐπεπήγει οὐ βέβαιος ἐν αὐτῇ ὥστ᾽ ἐπελθεῖν, … καὶ ἡ νὺξ … ὑπονειφομένη πολὺ τὸ ὕδωρ … ἐπεποιήκει

even the last of Plataeans got over the ditch, though not without effort and difficulty; as ice had formed in it, not strong enough to walk upon, and the snow that had fallen during the night, had made the water deep

div.head: §PperfImm Pluperfect of Immediate OccurrenceSmyth 1953, CGCG 33.53
div.p: The pluperfect may denote that a past action occurred so immediately or suddenly that it was accomplished almost at the same moment as another action.

cit.quote: ὡς δὲ ἐλήφθησαν, ἐλέλυντο αἱ σπονδαί
and when they were captured the truce was (already) at an end (the fact of their capture was equivalent to the immediate rupture of the truce).
ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἅπαξ ἤρξαντο ὑπείκειν, ταχὺ δὴ πᾶσα ἡ ἀκρόπολις ἔρημος τῶν πολεμίων ἐγεγένητο
And when they had once begun to give way, speedily the whole Acropolis had become bare of the enemy

div.head: §PperfInt Intensive PluperfectCGCG 33.42
div.p: Similar to the perfect tense, pluperfect with certain atelic verbs such as φοβέομαι or θαυμάζω might indicate an intensive interpretation.

cit.quote: ἔξω … οἱ τῶν Ἀρκάδων ὁπλῖται παντάπασιν οὐκ ἀντεξῇσαν: οὕτω τοὺς πελταστὰς ἐπεφόβηντο
the hoplites of the Arcadians did not come out at all to meet them; such fear they felt for the peltasts

div.head: §Futperf Future Completed ActionSmyth 1955-1956 & 581 & 600, CGCG 33.46
div.p: The future perfect denotes a future state resulting from a completed action: ἀναγεγράψομαι I shall stand enrolled, δεδήσεται he shall be kept in prison.

cit.quote: the door will be kept shut
Some other woman will possess you

div.p: Most future perfects are middle in form, passive in meaning. The active future perfect is usually periphrastic, meaning that it is formed by combining the perfect active participle with ἔσομαι shall be; for instance, γεγραφὼς ἔσομαι I shall have written. Exceptions are two perfects with a present meaning, ἕστηκα I stand (ἵστημι set) and τέθνηκα I am dead (θνῄσκω), which form the future perfects ἑστήξω I shall stand, τεθνήξω I shall be dead.

cit.quote: we shall have determined on our duty

div.head: §FutperfInten Intensive or Immediate ConsequenceSmyth 1956, CGCG 33.47
div.p: When stress is laid upon complete fulfillment, the future perfect may imply rapidity, immediate consequence, or certainty, of action accomplished in the future.

cit.quote: φράζε, καὶ πεπράξεται
speak, and it shall be done instanter
εὐθὺς Ἀριαῖος ἀφεστήξει: ὥστε φίλος ἡμῖν οὐδεὶς λελείψεται
Ariaeus will soon withdraw, so that we shall have no friend left

div.head: §Act Active VoiceSmyth 1703-1712 & 920, CGCG 35.1-2
div.p: The active voice represents the subject as performing the action of the verb: λούω I wash. Under action is included being, as ἡ ὁδὸς μακρά ἐστι the way is long.

Active verbs may be transitive or intransitive. Verbs capable of taking a direct object are called transitive and other verbs are intransitive. Many verbs are used in the active voice both transitively and intransitively. The distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is a grammatical convenience, and is not founded on an essential difference of nature.

cit.quote: I have been long wondering
he shall receive a talent as his reward
I see the man
Clearchus was an exile

div.p: The active may be causative, and used of an action performed at the bidding of the subject:

cit.quote: Cyrus burnt down the palace (i.e. had it burnt down)

div.head: §MidIndir Indirect Reflexive MiddleSmyth 1719-1722 & 1725 & 1728, CGCG 35.8-10, Allan (2003): p.112-117
div.p: In the indirect reflexive middle, the subject of the verb is affected by the verb, often as a beneficiary. The Indirect Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting for himself, with reference to himself, or with something belonging to himself. Self is often the indirect object. So πορίζεσθαι provide for oneself (πορίζειν provide), φυλάττεσθαι guard against (φυλάττειν keep guard), αἱρεῖσθαι choose (take for oneself). The middle often denotes that the subject acts with something belonging to himself (material objects, means, powers). It is often used for acts done willingly.

cit.quote: to procure arms for themselves
he sent for hoplites
I married

div.p: Some middle verbs may indicate that the subject has something done by another for himself. This use is often called the causative middle.

cit.quote: for I had you taught this
to have food served up
ὅσοι ὅπλα ἀφῄρηνται, ταχὺ ἄλλα ποιήσονται
all who have had their arms taken from them will soon get others made
he had a tent prepared for himself

div.head: §MidDir Direct Reflexive MiddleSmyth 1717-1718 & 1724, CGCG 35.11-12, Allan (2003): p.88-95
div.p: The Direct Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting directly on themselves. Self is here the direct object. Direct reflexive middle verbs often express external and natural acts, such as grooming: ἀλείφεσθαι anoint oneself or λοῦσθαι wash oneself. The part affected may be added in the accusative.

cit.quote: He has not bathed since his birth

div.p: “ἐπαίσατο τὸν μηρόν” X. C. 7.3.6; ⇾ he smote his thigh
The reflexive pronoun may be used with the middle often for emphasis:
“ἑαυτὸν ἀποκρύπτεσθαι” P. R. 393c; ⇾ to hide himself

div.head: §MidSpee Speech Act MiddleCGCG 35.27, Allan (2003): p.105-112
div.p: Verbs expressing certain kinds of speech are often middle-only. Most speech act middle verbs have a rather specific lexical meaning, while more general or neutral verbs of saying tend to be active.

The subject of a speech act middle could be involved in the speech act in different ways, for example, as a beneficiary or an experiencer. Some middle verbs of speech may indicate a strong emotional or mental involvement of the subject.

cit.quote: but on the tenth Achilles called the people to assembly
But I will speak out to you, and will swear thereto a mighty oath
So spoke the son of Peleus
He with good intent addressed the gathering and spoke among them

div.head: §MidMotion Body MotionsSmyth 1729, CGCG 35.17, Allan (2003): p.76-84
div.p: The middles of body motion represent the subject changing their physical state voluntarily, thus being both the agent and the patient; for instance, ἅλλεσθαι jump, πέτεσθαι fly or ὀρχεῖσθαι dance. Under this category belongs the middle of collective motion. The middle of collective motion is used for verbs express a change of position of a group, such as gathering.

cit.quote: θάμβησεν δ᾽ Ἀχιλεύς, μετὰ δ᾽ ἐτράπετ᾽, αὐτίκα δ᾽ ἔγνω Παλλάδ᾽ Ἀθηναίην
Achilles was seized with wonder, and turned around, and immediately recognized Pallas Athene.
… and came to the tents and the ships of the Myrmidons.
οἳ μὲν ἐκήρυσσον, τοὶ δ᾽ ἠγείροντο μάλ᾽ ὦκα
they made summons, and the men gathered full quickly.
the man would do a somersault into a ring of knives; he would jump into fire.

div.head: §MidMent Mental Activity, Process or PerceptionCGCG 35.27 & 35.17, Allan (2003): p.101-105
div.p: Middle verbs of mental activity or process indicate intentional or unintentional involvement of a subject in a mental or emotional activity; for instance, βούλομαι want or prefer, ἥδομαι enjoy or be glad, ἡγέομαι believe or consider. The subject could be involved in the verb as the agent or the experiencer.

The crucial difference between the mental activity and the mental process type is that mental activities are intentional while the mental process is unintentional. However, many verbs may indicate both mental processes and activities. Verbs of perception are also included in this category, expressing intentional or unintentional perception of a subject through their sensory organs.

cit.quote: … who might say why Phoebus Apollo is so angry.
listening to the singer
οἱ Ἕλληνες δρησμὸν βουλεύονται καταρρωδηκότες …
the Hellenes are planning flight in their fear …

div.head: §MidRecip Reciprocal MiddleSmyth 1726-1727, CGCG 35.24, Allan (2003): p.84-88
div.p: Reciprocal middle verbs involve events that naturally need more than one participant, acting toward each other in the same manner, meaning that the relation between each participant to the other one is the same; for instance, with verbs of contending, conversing (questioning, replying), greeting, embracing, etc. The reciprocal middle is often found with compounds of διά.

cit.quote: the athletes contended
when they had got into position they fought
they conversed man with man
to have friendly intercourse with one another
they will divide this up among themselves

div.head: §MidSpon Spontaneous Process MiddleCGCG 35.17, Allan (2003): p.60-64
div.p: The subjects of spontaneous process middle verbs go through internal, physical changes of state without initiating it directly. The importance difference from passive is that in spontaneous process middles the agent is unknown or unidentifiable. Most middles of this type also have a causative counterpart in the active voice; for instance, ἀπόλλυμαι perish and ἀπόλλυμι destroy.

cit.quote: (...) πέλας τῶν κήπων (...), ἐν τοῖσι φύεται αὐτόματα ῥόδα
(...) near the gardens (...), where roses grow of themselves
and constantly the pyres of the dead burned thick.

div.head: §Pass Passive voiceSmyth 1735-1752 & 814, CGCG 35.1, Allan (2003): p. 58-60
div.p: The passive voice represents the subject as acted on. The passive has been developed from the middle. With the exception of some futures and the aorist, the middle forms do duty as passives: αἱρεῖται takes for himself, i.e. chooses, and is chosen; κέχυται has poured itself, has been poured. The agent of the passive is regularly expressed by ὑπό and the genitive; sometimes by ἀπό, διά, ἐκ, παρά, πρός with the genitive, or by ὑπό with the dative (in poetry).

cit.quote: ἐώθουν, ἐωθοῦντο, ἔπαιον, ἐπαίοντο
they pushed, were pushed, they struck, were struck
envied by Odysseus
they did not think it right to be governed by us

div.p: The passive may have the sense allow oneself to be, get oneself:

cit.quote: carrying and allowing ourselves to be carried across the border

div.p: The dative, or a prepositional phrase, is regularly used with the passive to denote the instrument, means, or cause. The agent may be viewed as the instrument. The instrument of an action, when regarded as the agent, is personified, and may be expressed by ὑπό with the genitive.

cit.quote: he is captured by a trireme

div.head: §Ind Assertions and QuestionsSmyth 1771-1773 & 2300 & 2189 & 2203, CGCG 34.5 & 54.1-2
div.p: The indicative states particular or general suppositions, makes affirmative or negative assertions and expressing beliefs, facts or assumptions. The indicative is also used for expressing requests, suggestions and questions.

cit.quote: Clearchus was an exile
τί δὲ ἵππων οἴει;
but what do you think of horses?

div.p: In assumptions:

cit.quote: ἐξήμαρτέ τις ἄκων: συγγνώμη ἀντὶ τιμωρίας τούτῳ
suppose someone involuntarily committed an offence; for him there is pardon rather than punishment

div.p: The indicative may be used to express a doubtful assertion about a present or past action (negative μή or μὴ οὐ). Such sentences are often regarded as questions with the effect of doubtful affirmation.

cit.quote: ἀλλ᾽ ἄρα . . . μὴ ὁ Κτήσιππος ἦν ὁ ταῦτ᾽ εἰπών
but I suspect (i.e. perhaps) after all it was Ctesippus who said this
but perhaps we did not do well in agreeing to this

div.p: The indicative mood is frequently used in different types of subordinate clause, including temporal, conditional or relative clauses. The indicative in the subordinate clause may indicate a general assumption or statement, or it may be a modal indicative, for instance, in relative or conditional clauses referring to a counterfactual action.

cit.quote: it was plain that the king was somewhere hard by
nor are they maintained for any other single purpose than for fighting (lit. how they shall fight)

div.head: §IndOblig Unfulfilled ObligationSmyth 1774- 1779, CGCG 34.17, Gildersleeve 364
div.p: With impersonal verbs indicating obligation, propriety, necessity, or possibility, the indicative without ἄν is used to express an unfulfilled obligation. Such expressions are ἔδει, χρῆν (or ἐχρῆν), προσῆκε, καιρὸς ἦν, ἄξιον ἦν, εἰκὸς ἦν, δίκαιον ἦν, αἰσχρὸν ἦν, ἐξῆν, καλῶς εἶχεν, verbals in -τόν or -τέον with ἦν, etc. Here, the indicative denotes that an action contrary to what has happened (often expressed by an infinitive) was or is required. This use of the indicative is a variation of the counterfactual indicative.

cit.quote: I ought to have taken the pledges then
it would have been worth hearing
he might have remained
τί σιγᾷς; οὐκ ἐχρῆν σιγᾶν
why art thou silent? Thou shouldst not be silent
these men ought not to be alive

div.head: §IndWish Unattainable WishSmyth 1780-1783, CGCG 34.18 & 38.40, Gildersleeve 367
div.p: The past indicative with εἴθε or with εἰ γάρ, without ἄν, is used to express a present or past wish which cannot be realized. The imperfect refers to present time, the aorist to past time (negative μή).

cit.quote: would that thou hadst (now) a better heart
would that I had then been with thee

div.p: An unattainable wish may also be expressed by ὤφελον (ought) with the present or aorist infinitive:

cit.quote: would that Cyrus were (now) alive (Cyrus ought to be alive)
would that the multitude were able to do evil

div.head: §IndCount Counterfactual IndicativeSmyth 1784-1789, CGCG 34.15-16
div.p: The indicative of the historical tenses with ἄν (κέν) may indicate counterfactual (or unreal) actions. The imperfect refers to the present or the past, the aorist to the past (rarely to the present), the pluperfect to the present (less commonly to the past). This use of the indicative with ἄν undicating unreality is closely connected to past potential use of the indicative. The past potential use of the indicative with ἄν (κέν) expresses past potentiality, probability (cautious statement), or necessity.

cit.quote: but the case would then have been decided on its own merits
and in that case it were far better
I should have liked Simon to be (or I wish Simon were) of the same mind as myself
which they could not have expected
τίς γὰρ ἂν ᾠήθη ταῦτα γενέσθαι;
for who would have expected these things to happen?
one might (could, would) have known
fear might have seized even a man of stout heart

div.head: §SubjHort Hortatory SubjunctiveSmyth 1797-1799 & 1809, CGCG 34.6
div.p: The hortatory subjunctive (present or aorist) is used to express a request or a proposal (negative μή). The hortatory use of the subjunctive compensates for the absence of an imperative of the first person and is more common in the first person plural than first person singular.

cit.quote: let us go now and hear the man
let's not go there yet
come, let us consider
let me now speak about the bill

div.head: §SubjProh Prohibitive SubjunctiveSmyth 1800, CGCG 34.7
div.p: The subjunctive (in the second and third persons of the aorist) is often used to express prohibitions (negative μή). The third person is less common and usually represents the second person (see example below).

cit.quote: do not lose heart
and let no one suppose ( \= μὴ ὑπολάβητε do not suppose).

div.p: οὐ μή with the subjunctive of the second person in the dramatic poets occasionally expresses a strong prohibition:

cit.quote: don't talk nonsense

div.head: §SubjDoubt Doubtful AssertionSmyth 1801-1804, CGCG 34.10
div.p: The present subjunctive with μή may express a doubtful assertion, with μὴ οὐ a doubtful negation. The idea of apprehension or anxiety (real or assumed) is due to the situation. A touch of irony often marks this use, which is chiefly Platonic. With μή (of what may be true):

cit.quote: I suspect it's rather bad form (lit. too rude) to tell the truth
but I rather think this may not be so
virtue is perhaps not a thing to be taught

div.p: In Homer μή with the independent subjunctive is used to indicate fear and warning, or to suggest danger:

cit.quote: may he not (as I fear he may) in his anger do aught to injure the sons of the Achaeans

div.head: §SubjDelib Deliberative SubjunctiveSmyth 1804-1809, CGCG 34.8
div.p: The deliberative subjunctive (present or aorist) is used for expressing doubt of the speaker about what to do or say (negative μή). It is often used in the first person.

cit.quote: εἴπωμεν ἢ σιγῶμεν;
shall we speak or keep silence?
τί δράσω; ποῖ φύγω;
what am I to do? whither shall I fly?
μὴ φῶμεν;
shall we not say?

div.p: The subjunctive question does not refer to a future fact, but to what is, under the present circumstances, advantageous or proper to do or say. βούλει, βούλεσθε (poet. θέλεις, θέλετε) often precede the subjunctive.

cit.quote: βούλει σοι εἴπω;
do you wish me to say to you?

div.head: §SubjHomer Anticipatory Subjunctive (Homeric)Smyth 1810- 1812
div.p: In Homer the subjunctive is often closely akin to the future indicative, and refers by anticipation to a future event (negative οὐ).

cit.quote: οὐ γάρ πω τοίους ἴδον ἀνέρας, οὐδὲ ἴδωμαι
for never yet saw I such men, nor shall I see them
and one will say

div.head: §SubjDenia Emphatic DenialSmyth 1804, CGCG 34.9
div.p: The subjunctive with οὐ μή can indicate an emphatic denial, expressing a strong belief that something will not happen.

cit.quote: the king will no longer be able to overtake us
I will not cease from searching for wisdom
he will certainly not obey

div.head: §SubjSubor In subordinate clauseSmyth 2481-3, 2487, CGCG 40.9, Gildersleeve 456
div.p: The subjunctive mood is frequently used in different types of subordinate clause, including temporal, conditional or relative clauses. Indefinite subjunctive with ἄν is used to represent actions that are occurring repeatedly or generically. Prospective subjunctive with ἄν indicates an action that is definitely or probably occurring in the future. Subjunctive dependent clauses regularly take ἄν except in the older language. The omission of ἄν is sometimes due to clerical error, sometimes perhaps to a sense of euphony, sometimes to a survival of the older construction.

cit.quote: ὃς ἂν δακρῦσαι μάλιστα τὴν θύσασαν παραχρῆμα ποιήσῃ πόλιν, οὗτος τὰ νικητήρια φέρει
and the man that succeeds at once in drawing most tears from the sacrificing city carries off the palm of victory.
ὡς ἐγώ ὁπότερος ἂν σφῷν νῦν με μᾶλλον εὖ ποιῇ, τούτῳ παραδώσω τῆς πυκνὸς τὰς ἡνίας
to whichever of you shall treat me best I hand over the reins of state.

div.p: The present and aorist indicative and subjunctive (usually without ἄν) are regularly used in similes with ὡς, ὡς εἰ, ὡς εἴ τε as if, ὡς ὅτε, ὡς ὁπότε as when.

cit.quote: οἱ δ᾽, ὥς τ᾽ αἰγυπιοὶ . . . πέτρῃ ἐφ᾽ ὑψηλῇ μεγάλα κλάζοντε μάχωνται, ὣς οἱ κεκλήγοντες ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλοισιν ὄρουσαν
and they, like vultures who contend with loud screams on a lofty cliff, even so they rushed screaming against each other

div.head: §OptWish Optative of WishSmyth 1814-1819, CGCG 34.14, Monro 299
div.p: The optative without ἄν is used to express a wish referring to the future. (negative μή). The optative of wish, or cupitive optative, is often introduced by εἰ γάρ, εἴθε (Hom. αἰ γάρ, αἴθε), or by εἰ, ὡς (both poetical).

cit.quote: ὦ παῖ, γένοιο πατρὸς εὐτυχέστερος
ah, boy, mayest thou prove more fortunate than thy sire
may he perish
oh, if you would become our friend

div.p: The optative introduced by εἰ γάρ, etc. is sometimes explained as a protasis with the conclusion omitted:

cit.quote: would that it might happen

div.p: An unattainable wish, referring to the present, may be expressed by the present optative in Homer:

cit.quote: would that I were young again

div.p: Under wishes are included execrations and protestations:

cit.quote: may I perish

div.p: The optative may indicate rhetorical wishes, willingness, or indifferance as in imprecations.

cit.quote: into the fire let us cast all counsels and plans of warriors

div.head: §OptComm Command or RequestSmyth 1820 , CGCG 34.13, Monro 299
div.p: The optative may express a command, exhortation, or request in the second-person with a force nearly akin to the imperative. In the first-person, it is used to express compliance to a wish or command or taking permission to do something.

cit.quote: let Chirisophus lead
I will speak then

div.head: §OptPoten Potential OptativeSmyth 1821-1834, CGCG 34.13
div.p: The potential optative with ἄν states a future possibility, propriety, or likelihood. The potential optative, which in Attic regularly takes ἄν, is occasionally found in Homer and later poetry in an earlier form, without that particle. The potential optative is sometimes used to soften the statement of an opinion or fact, or to express irony.

cit.quote: you may see that this is so
all would agree
I (would gladly ask) should like to ask
thou canst not take
I will tell this
quicker than a man could speak

div.head: §OptSubor In subordinate clauseSmyth 2186-87 & 1824, CGCG 40. 9 & 40.12-15
div.p: The optative mood is frequently used in different types of subordinate clause, including temporal, conditional or relative clauses. In subordinate clauses in the secondary or historic sequence, the optative may replace the original mood. This use of optative is limited to the subordinate clauses of the secondary sequence (imperfect, aorist, pluperfect) and does not appear in primary sequence (present, perfect, future) and is called the oblique optative. The indefinite subordinate clauses of historic sequence may use the iterative optative (without ἄν) to express a habitual or repeated action.

cit.quote: εἴ πού τι ὁρῴη βρωτόν, διεδίδου
if ever he saw anything to eat anywhere, he always distributed it
εἰ δέ τις καὶ ἀντείποι, εὐθὺς . . . ἐτεθνήκει
but if any one even made an objection, he was promptly put to death
δέομαι οὖν σου παραμεῖναι ἡμῖν: ὡς ἐγὼ οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἑνὸς ἥδιον ἀκούσαιμι ἢ σοῦ
accordingly I beg you to stay with us; because there is no one (in my opinion) to whom I should more gladly listen than to you.
you are so far unworthy of compassion that you would be detested most justly of all men
εἰ δέ τινες φοβοῦνται μὴ ματαία ἂν γένοιτο αὕτη ἡ κατασκευή, εἰ πόλεμος ἐγερθείη, ἐννοησάτω ὅτι κτλ.
if some are afraid that this condition of things may prove vain, if war should arise, let them (him) consider that, etc.

div.p: When an optative of the principal clause refers to future time (potential optative and optative of wish), the subordinate clause takes the optative by assimilation.

cit.quote: would that every man would practise the craft that he understood
ὄλοιο μήπω, πρὶν μάθοιμι
perish not yet . . . until I learn

div.head: §ImprComm Command or ProhibitionSmyth 1835-1844, CGCG 34.19
