div.p: Under commands are included requests, entreaties, summons, prescriptions, exhortations, etc. All imperative tenses refer to the future. The negative with the imperative verbs is μή and indicates prohibition. In exhortations ἄγε, φέρε, ἴθι (usually with δή, sometimes with νύν), often precede the imperative.

cit.quote: τὰ μὲν ποίει, τὰ δὲ μὴ ποίει
do this and refrain from doing that
come listen
go now, take your supper
but come, say
don't be astonished
don't raise a disturbance
let no one tell me
let no one be ignorant of this fact
let him neither acquit nor condemn in any way

div.head: §ImprAssum Assumption, Concession or GreetingSmyth 1839, CGCG 34.20
div.p: The imperative may be used in many different expressions, including assumptions (hypothetical imperative), to make a concession, or to grant permission. The imperative is commonly used in greetings and curses.

cit.quote: let it be assumed as far as I am concerned
assume it to be as you say
οὐκοῦν κείσθω ταῦτα;
shall these points be established?
yet, even so fare thee well
go to hell!

div.head: §InfDyn Dynamic infinitivePedalion 573, CGCG 51.8-18, Smyth 2008-2011
div.p: The dynamic infinitive expresses an action, and complements verbs with meaning of want, desire, force, ask, command, try, teach, etc. The dynamic infinitive indicates a potential action, which may or may not be realized. The prolative infinitive which complement verbs that take an infinitive as the object are dynamic infinitives. Dynamic infinitives, among other uses, can indicate purpose, result, or limit the meaning of an adjective or a noun.
The tenses of this infinitive are purely aspectual, and denote only the stage of action. The negative of dynamic infinitive is μή, while the negative of declarative infinitive is οὐ.

cit.quote: τί χρὴ ποιεῖν;
what must be done?
a good education teaches obedience to the laws
he taught you to distinguish the good and the bad
able to assist us
they planned to leave the city
the king asks that you sail away
he gave this land over to the Greeks to plunder
Ἀριστάρχῳ . . . ἔδοτε ἡμέραν ἀπολογήσασθαι
you granted a day to Aristarchus to make his defence
I offer myself to be questioned
they turned back to the city before they attempted to scale the wall

div.head: §InfDec Declarative infinitiveCGCG 51.19-27, Smyth 2016-2024, Pedalion 622
div.p: The declarative infinitive expresses a belief, idea, or speech about an action in indirect discourse. Common verbs that take a declarative infinitive are φημί, λέγω, νομίζω, δοκέω, ἀγγέλλω, etc.

Unlike dynamic infinitives, declarative infinitives are considered to have relative temporal value. The present tense often indicates that the action is simultanious with the main verb, the future tense indicates posteriority, while the aorist tense is used for expressing anteriority. The perfect tense often indicates a state that is simultaneous with the verb of speech or opinion.
The declarative infinitive modified by ἄν has a potential meaning similar to potential optative (Note that the dynamic infinitive never takes ἄν).
The negative of declarative infinitive is οὐ, however, in some cases an emphatic μή is used.

cit.quote: they assert that they are loyal
nobody said that he knew him
the guides say there is no other road
everybody in time to come will say that there is nothing more profitable than bravery
the king thinks he is victorious,
I think it is best
they suspected that they were to go against the king
(Σωκράτης) τὸ ἀγνοεῖν ἑαυτὸν ἐγγυτάτω . . . μανίας ἐλογίζετο εἶναι
Socrates was of the opinion that for a man not to know himself was very near to madness

div.head: §InfIdio Idiomatic expressionsSmyth 2012, CGCG 51.49, Pedalion 648
div.p: Certain idiomatic infinitives are used in parenthetical phrases to limit the application of a single expression or of the entire sentence. This is common with verbs of saying. In these constructions, the infinitive is used absolutely and is not dependant on any other words in the sentence.

cit.quote: not one word of truth, I may say, did they utter
in a word the State gained no advantage

div.p: Especially common is the absolute εἶναι in ἑκὼν willingly, intentionally, if you can help it, usually in negative or quasi-negative statements (ἑκών may be inflected). Some other expressions are ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν, ὡς ἐμοὶ κρῖναι, (ὡς) εἰκάσαι, (ὡς) ἀκοῦσαι, ὀλίγου δεῖν, μικροῦ δεῖν, etc.

cit.quote: nor do you intentionally cause strangers to laugh
it is not willingly separated
τό γε ἐπ᾽ ἐκεῖνον εἶναι ἐσώθης (ἄν)
so far, at least, as it depended on him you would have been saved
ὁ γὰρ Κτήσιππος ἔτυχε πόρρω καθεζόμενος τοῦ Κλεινίου, ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν
for Ctesippus, it seems to me, happened to be sitting at a distance from Clinias
almost three talents

div.head: §InfComm Infinitive of Commands, Wishes, and ExclamationsSmyth 2013-2015, Pedalion 582 & 583, CGCG 51.47-48
div.p: A dynamic infinitive can be used for commands, instead of the second person of the imperative. The person addressed is regarded as the subject. This infinitive is more common in poetry than in prose.

cit.quote: θαρσῶν νῦν, Διόμηδες, ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι
with good courage now, Diomed, fight against the Trojans
σὺ δέ, Κλεαρίδα . . . τὰς πύλας ἀνοίξας ἐπεκθεῖν
but do you, Clearidas, open the gates and sally forth

div.p: The infinitive with a subject accusative may be used in the sense of the optative of wish.

cit.quote: θεοὶ πολῖται, μή με δουλείας τυχεῖν
ye gods of my country, may bondage not be my lot!
ὦ Ζεῦ, ἐκγενέσθαι μοι Ἀθηναίους τείσασθαι
oh Zeus, that it be granted to me to punish the Athenians!

div.p: The infinitive is often used in exclamations of surprise or indignation. The subject stands in the accusative.

cit.quote: that I should suffer this!
to keep a dog like that!

div.head: §InfArt Articular InfinitiveSmyth 2025-2037, CGCG 51.38-46, Pedalion 826 & 621 & 735
div.p: The infinitive in combination with a neuter singular article can function as a noun phrase. The articular infinitive, while having the character of a noun, retains the functions of a verb. The articular infinitive can be used similar to any other noun phrase and admits the constructions of an ordinary noun. It may indicate time (after verbs of saying or thinking), or may be timeless. The case is indicated by the article:
Nom. τὸ ποιεῖν making or to make, τὸ ποιήσειν, τὸ ποιῆσαι, τὸ πεποιηκέναι
Gen. τοῦ ποιεῖν of making, τοῦ ποιήσειν, τοῦ ποιῆσαι, etc.
Dat. τῷ ποιεῖν for making, by making, τῷ ποιήσειν, τῷ ποιῆσαι, etc.
Acc. τὸ ποιεῖν, τὸ ποιήσειν, τὸ ποιῆσαι, etc.
The negative of the articular infinitive is μή.

cit.quote: τὸ Πελοποννησίους αὐτοῖς μὴ βοηθῆσαι παρέσχεν ὑμῖν . . . Σαμίων κόλασιν
the fact that the Peloponnesians did not come to their assistance enabled you to punish the Samians
from desire to drink
having gained the greatest amount of courage
τί οὖν ἐστιν . . . τοῦ τοῖς φίλοις ἀρήγειν κάλλιον;
what then is nobler than to help one's friends?
we desisted from weeping
ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐπὶ Καρίαν ἰέναι . . . ἐπὶ Φρυγίας ἐπορεύετο
instead of going against Caria, he marched toward Phrygia
without exercising self-control
ἵνα . . . ἀπιστῶσι τῷ ἐμὲ τετιμῆσθαι ὑπὸ δαιμόνων
that they may distrust my having been honoured by divine powers
I commend speed to thee
when I am informed, I will not refuse the deed

div.head: §PartAttr Attributive and Substantival ParticipleSmyth 2049-2053 & 1166 & 1153, CGCG 52.46-49
div.p: The attributive participle (with any modifier), with or without the article, modifies a noun like any other adjective. The noun with which the attributive participle (with the article) agrees directly, may be omitted, and as a result, the participle becomes a noun. Such participial nouns appear in active, middle, and passive forms, and admit the distinctions of tense. A participle noun may be modified by adjectives or take a genitive when its verbal nature has ceased to be felt. Neuter participles are often substantival, as τὰ δέοντα duties.

cit.quote: the danger impending over the State
the existing enemies
the mountain called Cotylaeum
those who shall be willing to remain
whoever wants to go home
the one who gave this opinion
the man who took this position in the State was I
the petty interests of the State

div.head: §PartCirc Circumstantial ParticipleSmyth 2054-2067, CGCG 52.29-31 & 52.34-45
div.p: The circumstantial participle is added, without the article, to a noun or pronoun to set forth some circumstance under which an action, generally the main action, takes place. The circumstantial participle thus qualifies the principal verb of the sentence like an adverbial clause or supplementary predicate. The circumstantial participle expresses simply circumstance or manner in general. It may imply various other relations, such as time, manner, means, cause, purpose, concession, condition, etc. It is often impossible to assign a participle exclusively to any one of these relations (which are purely logical), nor can all the delicate relations of the participle be set forth in systematic form.

If the subject of the participle is not identical with the noun or pronoun subject or object of the leading verb, it forms an absolute participle clause of either genitive or accusative absolute (Explained under PartGen. and PartAcc.)

cit.quote: (οἱ ἄνθρωποι) λιπόντες τὴν ὁδὸν φεύγοντες ὀλίγοι ἀπέθνῃσκον
by leaving the road and making off only a few were killed
as I said at the outset
at last he became angry

div.p: Expressing Manner:

cit.quote: they marched past in order
hurry up and open
he sailed out unobserved by the guard

div.p: Expressing means:

cit.quote: they live by pillaging

div.p: Expressing cause:

cit.quote: Παρύσατις . . . ὑπῆρχε τῷ Κύρῳ, φιλοῦσα αὐτὸν μᾶλλον ἢ τὸν βασιλεύοντα Ἀρταξέρξην
Parysatis favoured Cyrus because she loved him more than she did Artaxerxes the king
they held aloof from gains because they thought them disgraceful
τί γὰρ δεδιότες σφόδρα οὕτως ἐπείγεσθε;
for what are you afraid of, that you are so desperately in haste?

div.p: Expressing purpose or object, typically in the future tense:

cit.quote: having sent a herald in advance to proclaim war
they summoned from all the cities men to listen to the letter from the king

div.p: Expressing any attendant circumstance:

cit.quote: having collected an army he laid siege to Miletus
he arrives with an army

div.head: §PartGen Circumstantial Participle - Genitive AbsoluteSmyth 2068-2075, CGCG 52.32
div.p: A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence, stands in the genitive absolute. The subject of the participle in the genitive absolute construction is different than the subject of the main verb and it should be expressed separately, therefore, both the participle and its subject stand in the genitive, forming a genitive absolute construction. Like other circumstantial participles, the genitive absolute expresses time, cause, condition, concession, or simply any attendant circumstance.

cit.quote: these things were effected while Conon was in command
this said, they rose
Ἠϊόνα . . . Μήδων ἐχόντων πολιορκίᾳ εἷλον
they blockaded and captured Eïon which was held by the Medes
by the enfeebling of the body, the spirit too is made weaker
even though he is sending for me, I am unwilling to go
Cyrus ascended the mountains without opposition (lit. no one hindering) (or since no one opposed him).

div.head: §PartAcc Circumstantial Participle - Accusative AbsoluteSmyth 2076-2078, CGCG 52.33
div.p: The accusative absolute is an impersonal participe in accusative singular neuter form that does not agree with a subject. When the participle is impersonal, or has an infinitive as its subject, it stands in the accusative absolute, instead of the genitive. Such participles have no apparent grammatical connection with the rest of the sentence.

cit.quote: οὐδεὶς τὸ μεῖζον κακὸν αἱρήσεται ἐξὸν τὸ ἔλαττον (αἱρεῖσθαι)
no one will choose the greater evil when it is possible to choose the less
ἧς (βουλῆς) νῦν ἀξιοῖ τυχεῖν οὐ μετὸν αὐτῷ
to which he now claims admission though he has no right
for of course you know because it concerns you
μετεμέλοντο ὅτι μετὰ τὰ ἐν Πύλῳ, καλῶς παρασχόν, οὐ ξυνέβησαν
they repented that after what had occurred at Pylos, although a favourable occasion had presented itself, they had not come to terms
a command having been given (it having been commanded) me by the people to convey Menon to the Hellespont
σὲ οὐχὶ ἐσώσαμεν . . . οἷόν τε ὂν καὶ δυνατόν
we did not rescue you although it was both feasible and possible

div.p: The participle of a personal verb may be used absolutely if it is preceded by ὡς or ὥσπερ. Examples:

cit.quote: ηὔχετο πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς τἀγαθὰ διδόναι, ὡς τοὺς θεοὺς κάλλιστα εἰδότας ὁποῖα ἀγαθά ἐστι
(Socrates) prayed to the gods that they would give him good things, in the belief that the gods know best what sort of things are good
σιωπῇ ἐδείπνουν, ὤσπερ τοῦτο προστεταγμένον αὐτοῖς
they were supping in silence just as if this had been enjoined upon them

div.head: §PartSupp Supplementary ParticipleSmyth 2088-2119, CGCG 52.8-28
div.p: The supplementary participle completes the idea of the verb by showing that to which its action relates. The supplementary participle agrees either with the subject or with the object of the main verb; with the subject when the verb is intransitive or passive, with the object when the verb is transitive.

cit.quote: I never ceased pitying ourselves
I put a stop to the poor being wronged
I proved that Philip was acting unjustly
he will straightway be proved to be ridiculous

div.p: With verbs of emotion (rejoicing and grieving) the participle often denotes cause.

cit.quote: I like to converse with very old men
I am not content to live on these conditions
I should not be annoyed at learning
they took it hard at abandoning their homes
I do not repent having made such a defence

div.head: §ArtPart Particular articleSmyth 1118-1120, CGCG 28.1-4
div.p: The article ὁ, ἣ, τό marks something or someone as identifiable and known. The particular article denotes individual persons or things as distinguished from others of the same kind, and is used with someone or something that is well known, are already mentioned or in the mind of the speaker or writer, is particularized by an attributive or by the following description, or marked as usual or proper under the circumstances. In Greek, there is no indefinite article; therefore, lack of a definite article functions as an indefinite article.
The article is used when reference is made to a person or thing that is considered to be well known, and therefore is identifiable.

cit.quote: take the book
wishing to fight the battle
the people of the Athenians
λέγε τὴν ἐπιστολήν, ἣν ἔπεμψεν
read the letter that he sent
the prosecutor did not get the (requisite) part of the votes
(ὑμῖν) ἡ σχολή
your usual idleness

div.head: §ArtSubs As SubstantivizerSmyth 1153 & 1124 & 2052, CGCG 28.23-25
div.p: When the article is added to a word or word group other than a noun, it is substantivised. The article has the power to make a noun of any word or words to which it is prefixed. It can be used with adjectives, participles, prepositional phrases, adverbs, attributive genitives, and whole word groups, sentences and clauses.

cit.quote: the enactors of the laws are the weak men and the multitude
is on the side of the people/He favors the people’s side.
those in power, the government
those in the prime of life
the condition of the soldiers
the outbursts of wrath
you will not be in want of those who will be willing to encounter danger for you

div.head: §ArtPron PronominalSmyth 1100-1117, CGCG 28.26-31
div.p: Greek articles originally were demonstrative pronouns and the transition from the demonstrative to the article is so gradual that it is often impossible to distinguish between the two in earlier texts. In Homer ὁ, ἡ, τό is usually a demonstrative pronoun and is used substantively or adjectively; it also serves as the personal pronoun of the third person; however, the pronominal use of article is not common in classical Greek and survives mainly in connection with particles (μέν, δέ, γέ, τοί; and with καί preceding ὁ).

cit.quote: but I marvel at this
but her I will not release
τεύχεα δ᾽ ἐξενάριξε, τά οἱ πόρε χάλκεος Ἄρης
he stripped off the arms that brazen Ares had given him
οἱ μὲν ἐπορεύοντο, οἱ δ᾽ εἵποντο
the one party proceeded, the other followed
τοὺς μὲν ἀπέκτεινε, τοὺς δ᾽ ἐξέβαλεν
some he put to death, and others he expelled
οἱ μέν τινες ἀπέθνῃσκον, οἱ δ᾽ ἔφευγον
some were killed, but others escaped

div.head: §ArtGener GenericSmyth 1122-24, CGCG 28.6
div.p: The generic article denotes an entire class as distinguished from other classes. Thus, ὁ ἄνθρωπος man (as distinguished from other beings), οἱ γέροντες the aged.

cit.quote: the (a) soldier should fear his commander rather than the enemy
the informer is a vile thing

div.p: In the singular the generic article makes a single object the representative of the entire class; in the plural it denotes all the objects belonging to a class. The generic article is especially common, in the plural, with adjectives used substantively. A participle with the article may also denote an entire class.

cit.quote: you will not be in want of those who will be willing to encounter danger for you
newsmongers
those who shall be willing to remain

div.head: §ArtAbst Abstract ConceptSmyth 1131-35, CGCG 28.7
div.p: Abstract nouns generally have the article:

cit.quote: valour rather than flight saves men's lives
ἡ σωφροσύνη … καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ φρόνησις μὴ καθαρμός τις ᾖ
self-restraint and wisdom itself may well be a kind of purification

div.p: However, the names of the virtues, vices, arts, sciences, occupations often omit the article.

cit.quote: τί σωφροσύνη, τί μανία;
what is temperance, what is madness?

div.head: §ArtProp Proper NamesSmyth 1136-42, CGCG 28.8
div.p: Proper names may take the article if they are previously mentioned or specially marked as well known. However, the use of articles with proper names depends on the style of the author.

cit.quote: τοὺς στρατιώτας αὐτῶν, τοὺς παρὰ Κλέαρχον ἀπελθόντας, εἴα Κῦρος τὸν Κλέαρχον ἔχειν
their soldiers who seceded to Clearchus, Cyrus allowed Clearchus to retain
Solon
the Heracleses

div.head: §ArtPoss PossessionSmyth 1121, CGCG 28.4
div.p: The article often takes the place of an unemphatic possessive pronoun when there is no doubt as to the possessor.

cit.quote: Cyrus leaped down from his chariot and put on his breastplate
for these are the questions regarding which you will now cast your votes.

div.head: §AutEmph EmphaticSmyth 1204-1208, CGCG 29.9
div.p: The pronoun αὐτός is intensive when it is standing alone in the nominative case, or in the predicate position with a noun, or in agreement with a pronoun, in any case. For instance, αὐτὸς ὁ ἀνήρ, ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτός the man himself, αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἀνδρός, τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτοῦ, etc.

cit.quote: the naked truth
the greater part of the place was strong in itself (without artificial fortification)
merely this
men who uninvited turn their arms even against those who do not ask their assistance
they (the Athenians) seized the land themselves

div.p: In Homer αὐτός denotes the principal person or thing, in opposition to what is subordinate, and is intensive by contrast:

cit.quote: the man himself and his attendant

div.head: §AutPron Personal PronounSmyth 1212, CGCG 29.7
div.p: When αὐτός is unemphatic and standing alone in the cases other than nominative, it has the meaning of the personal pronoun of the third person (him, her, it, them). This use of αὐτός as a personal pronoun always refers to someone or something that is already introduced.

cit.quote: they ordered her to depart
ἄρχει τις αὐτῶν ἢ 'πὶ τῷ πλήθει λόγος;
Does someone govern them, or does authority rest with the masses?

div.head: §AutIden IdenticalnessSmyth 1210, CGCG 29.8
div.p: After the article, in the attributive position, αὐτός in any case means same. Thus, ὁ αὐτὸς ἀνήρ, rarely (ὁ) ἀνὴρ ὁ αὐτός the same man.

cit.quote: in the same summer
these same things
the people who are continually making the same speeches about the same things
ἐγὼ μὲν ὁ αὐτός εἰμι, ἱμεῖς δὲ μεταβάλλετε
I am the same, it is you who change

div.p: With a proper name or a word denoting an individual, the article is omitted

cit.quote: Menon himself
in front of the Great King himself

div.head: §AutRefl ReflexiveSmyth 1228 & 1233, CGCG 29.19
div.p: Instead of the indirect ἑαυτοῦ, etc., the oblique cases of αὐτός may be used as a reflexive pronoun:

cit.quote: he tried to divert the Athenians from their anger against himself

div.p: When ἑαυτοῦ, etc. precede, αὐτοῦ, etc. are usual instead of the direct reflexive:

cit.quote: Socrates was wont to set forth his opinion to those who conversed with him”

div.head: §Agr AgreementSmyth 976 & 1030-1039
div.p: This tag is applied when a word has been assigned a certain case to correspond with another word, such as in attributive adjectives or appositives.

div.head: §GBP Governed by Preposition
